Moderator: A very warm welcome, everyone. Thank you for joining our earnings call for the quarter ended 
September 30, 2026. As always, we are going to do this earnings call with management video switched on. We 
welcome attendees to ask the question with their videos on or off, as they prefer. To ask a question, you can 
raise your hand through your Zoom dashboard. To ensure a seamless flow, participants will be promoted as 
panelists in advance. Today, from Paytm's management, we have with us Mr. Vijay Shekhar Sharma, Founder 
and CEO, Mr. Madhur Deora, President and Group CFO, and Mr. Anuj Mittal, Senior Vice President, Investor 
Relations. In today's call, some statements made may be forward-looking in nature. Actual events may differ 
materially from those anticipated in such forward-looking statements. This earnings call is scheduled for 45 
minutes. A replay of the call and transcript will be made available on the company's IR website subsequently. I 
would now like to invite our Founder and CEO, Mr. Vijay Shekhar Sharma, to share his opening remarks. Over to 

you, Vijay.​
  
Vijay Shekhar Sharma: Yeah. Hi. Thank you. Thank you. Good afternoon, everyone for joining us. I think this 
was an interesting quarter. We've clearly come out of this question of whether Paytm can make profit or not. 
And it's very clear the business model is now compounding from where we were, let's say last year or year 
before. It is fundamentally to acquire customers from payment and cross-selling financial services. Obviously, 
the biggest financial service India needs is credit. So helping small merchants which are our primary business 
drivers is our primary revenue model. 
 
 I actually created a business presentation of what we believe is our business. So I'll start this time, after a long 
time, by giving you a business presentation on how we think and how we work. And this was intended because 
we were growing some of the international businesses. So I started to make and think about how we believe 
that Paytm should be looked at. Obviously, small businesses are our forte, and small businesses are our game. 
So this is our purpose, and we build a financial system for the world's small businesses. Start from India, take 
them to the rest of the world. And we champion the shop on the street, the family business, the growing SME, 
everyone. And we solve the small business problem beyond payments.  
 
And as you know, we go beyond the payment device on the counter because we believe that this is the starting 
of the journey. We acquire using payment. Credit is what earns our money. Insurance and wealth deepen, and 
AI binds. And the question of what would you do with AI probably hits inside this message, where every 
payment starts, every relationship starts with payment. We go and acquire small, medium, large businesses. 
And payment flow underwrites credit. This is the critical thing that you will see in our business that we start 
from small payments to the large and depending on different states, we unlock the next state. And then we 
protect the owner, family, team, and shop. This is the expansion of our insurance bucket. And then idle cash 
earns. 
This is how we help them. Obviously, loan or mutual fund distribution comes here.  
 
This is something that we believe that we are building as our AI stack for small merchants. If you read it, it is 
something that all small businesses need to get, capabilities which large companies already have. And they 
don't have somebody to operate it, so the AI operates on their behalf. So we have started making some of 
these things, and some of the revenue starts showing up. We believe this is a future upside beyond financial 
services for our business. It'll take time, but I want to be sure that this is something that we capture in our 
business model long term. And this is really important for us that all of our functions, whether it is workflow or 
financial services, as you know, is AI-first, including the very fact that we code, generate, and so on. So whether 
it is onboarding or customer… 
 
[Audio interruption]  
 
Vijay Shekhar Sharma: Yeah, okay. I hope you can hear me better now. All right, thank you. AI-first, the brain 
works. Well, the point is that all of our business runs, I can't say one line item or another, and it is every line 
item works with AI first. And the best part is that even our sales team works. So who's the correct merchant to 
acquire, where the high yield is, or who is important to retain? This is decided by a machine, not just 
individuals. This is important. Paytm changed the cost of serving a small business into a profit. And that is what 
we probably have been out there proving that small businesses, serving them, can be profitable. And then, as 
you know it. And here it is. It starts from payment, credit, underwrite, and money flows into partners; pricing is 
visible; AI-first. And then we want to take it to the rest of the world. And that's it. With this, we will start 
inviting our friends on the questions. Yeah. 
 

Moderator: Thanks, Vijay. We will start a Q&A now. The first question is from Sachin Salgaonkar from Bank of 
America, followed by Manish Adukia from Goldman Sachs. Sachin, please go ahead with your question. 
 
Sachin Salgaonkar: Thanks, Anandita. Congrats, management, on another good set of numbers. I have three 
questions. First question, I wanted to follow up on the MDR implementation on UPI. You guys did mention in 
the shareholder letter 2.5 bps improvement on payment processing margin, let's say, over a period of two to 
three quarters. So two sub-questions out there. 
 
Number one, how do you think this will flow through to EBITDA? And number two, from an opportunity point 
of view, are you guys looking to incrementally scale, let's say, at the consumer side or the merchant side? 
Because now, perhaps, the incremental LTV by CAC is getting better. And in the past, I remember Madhur 
sounded a bit more cautious on competition picking up. So any incremental comments would be helpful from a 
competition point of view also. 
 
Vijay Shekhar Sharma: Second part, you said before the competition picks up, what was the question? 
 
Sachin Salgaonkar: Sorry, let me repeat it. First, Vijay, you know, 2.5 bps of payment processing margin, how do 
we think this will flow through to EBITDA margin? Do we see a full flow through EBITDA margin, or do we see 
some incremental investments because you will be now targeting more consumers or merchants? And general 
thoughts on competition, especially in this space with monetization picking up. 
 
Vijay Shekhar Sharma: Yeah. So Sachin, the answer is that this is a bottom-line accretive number, and it is an 
upside. And the plan for consumer acquisition does not change and deter because of this. We remain 
committed to acquiring a larger number of consumers. Consumer market share is ours to win. And I remain 
committed.And I'm surprised that we unlocked some shocking, surprising things that were restricting our 
growth. And they were not just internal. They were external, if you will. And I'm very happy to say this, that we 
are going to go all in on market share. And we call it a primary KPI for my team. So it is. And it is not dependent 
on MDR or not. Because in our business model, MDR is not factored in absolutely completely. We just tried, in 
fact, looking at the most conservative method. And then we found out 2.5 bps is something that we can make.  
 
Remember, there is more revenue in this business because there is a platform fee. Typically, consumer apps are 
putting it in the market. And there is an acquiring side platform fee that exists. When large merchants, which 
are very large negotiating powers, put a very low margin, then companies put platform fees, even on the 
acquiring side. So I'm going to say that the bps that we've quoted does not factor in any potential additional 
revenue of any platform side fees that could have been added. So this is the logical today's best-case scenario 
number that we know of. And in my opinion, this is bottom-line accretive. Because this is not the basis of our 
consumer acquisition. We will still stay as aggressive as the current number is, where we will acquire more 
consumers. And yes, the consumer acquisition is a very positive number for us. I rather want to tell you this, 
that the number of features, the capabilities, the way we are acquiring customers, is something which we are 
very happy about and very positive about it. 
 
Sachin Salgaonkar: Got it. Just a quick follow-up. When I do a quick math on FY28 at 2.5 bps, it does translate 
into incrementally close to 900 crores in terms of incremental EBITDA. Is the math ballpark correct? 
 
Madhur Deora: Yeah, so on our GMV, which is 28 lakh crores, at a current scale, 2.5 bps would give you 
something slightly more than 700 crores. So if you're looking at FY28 numbers, that sounds ballpark, right. We 
obviously do expect to grow GMV faster than the market, both on the consumer and merchant side. So 
hopefully there's some upside there as well. 
 

Sachin Salgaonkar: Got it very clear. The second question is on what you mentioned, as you're looking to offer 
an AI platform to enterprise merchants. Basis Vijay’s opening remark, I guess the focus is more towards smaller 
merchants. So should we consider the equivalent of a Tally in an AI world? And it would be great to get some 
colour. Are you thinking about this as a subscription model? What's your target base? And what kind of 
monetization would we expect? 
 
Vijay Shekhar Sharma: So I believe, Sachin, subscription plus transaction fee, one of the two or both will be 
applicable. So marketing is a very simple method. And we have started acquiring customers where we have put 
the platform fee. We are working with Meta and Google, actually rather Meta, where we are charging a 
monthly platform fee. And then we get some percentage of spend also. So all these models are showing up. 
You can factor in based on a certain percentage of our customers who are glass-door merchants. This is how we 
look at it. We'll be able to acquire, or we will be able to sell, some other AI service. So yes, it is for small 
businesses. For large businesses, we have something more brewing up. Hopefully we will announce it after 
some time. But right now we are focused on creating agents for small businesses. 
 
Sachin Salgaonkar: Got it. And logically, monetization should start picking up in six to nine months from now? 
 
Vijay Shekhar Sharma: Oh yeah, one year, which is three months already passed. So nine months plus three 
equals one year. Yeah. 
 
Sachin Salgaonkar: Got it. And last question, I just wanted to understand how we should think about the mix 
between DLG and non-DLG and how that could change over a period of time. And also would love to 
understand how the consumer loan is scaling versus the merchant loan right now, now that consumer loans 
have started to pick up. 
 
Vijay Shekhar Sharma: Yeah, I'll talk about consumer loan, merchant loan, first of all. One of the things, Sachin, 
we learned that we don't have, or rather, the consumer app business does not have any right to win in the 
consumer loan distribution business if you are putting additional risk-reward-based bonus, which we have in 
the merchant side. So we switched our business model completely towards distribution without requiring any 
upside off or any DLG to be given in consumer business. And I think that has shown us the result. We've been 
able to distribute a large amount of credit to the small or large consumer demands. We, in that category, can 
serve any size of ticket, and you can see the revenue. I mean, surprisingly, I can only tell you, it has pleasantly 
surprised me also. The team has done phenomenally, phenomenally well, and we are going to go double all in 
and so on and so forth. So there is an opportunity. 
 
To the DLG mix, I'll ask Madhur to also chip in, but the simple answer is we don't look at the mix. We look at 
the more availability of capital, more availability of lenders and we want to have more number of people. And I 
always say this: if there is a new lender coming in, or if there is a lender there who wants to give us more 
capital because they want to take DLG, please take it. It is revenue-accretive and profitability-accretive because 
they open up more number of merchants, and the dollar value or the rupee value that they disburse. So it is 
overall in our business model, the one single downside is that it is a charge in the immediate month, but it is 
because we want to remain a credit distribution platform, never have anything which is future forward 
discounting of any revenue. So, as board guided, we have taken straight charge in the same quarter. 
 
So you will see that our revenues in that quarter will also have a cost because of the DLG reason, but it is 
overall as a business, it is rather a better business that there is no future forward discounting to be added in 
the revenue. Incidentally, it is a pure technology business, and we are happy to extend this, which gives us 
more revenue in the long term. Madhur, your point. 
 

Madhur Deora: Yeah, I think Vijay covered it. We don't say no to a lender just because they want DLG. We 
don't route more to a lender who has less DLG or no DLG. The idea is to find the right lender for the borrower 
and to do as much business as possible. Like we have mentioned consistently, even when DLG was going down 
or going up, we have consistently mentioned that we are largely indifferent to this. If a lender has a preference, 
we let them have the DLG, and it does back-end some of our profitability. 
 So that is worth pointing out when there's changes in DLG mix; it's worth pointing out to analysts just so that 
they get the kind of the models right, that some additional amount of our profitability is getting back-ended, 
right? And the final point I would just make is that we've been doing this for about two and a half years. So we 
do have some method to this, and we do know how to manage the DLGs quite well. And it has never really 
given us any negative surprises. So we're quite comfortable with running a large book within which a large 
percentage might be DLG-based. 
 
Sachin Salgaonkar: Thanks. And one last quick one. We are already at October end of October. There is a 
market cap of NPCI. Anything you're hearing from NPCI guys, key officials, if this would be implemented in 
December? 
 
Vijay Shekhar Sharma: We don't have the answer; NPCI might have the answer. We are the receivers. We don’t 
decide. 
 
Sachin Salgaonkar: Great, thanks a lot, guys.  
 
Vijay Shekhar Sharma: Thank you. 
 
Moderator: We will take the next question from Manish, followed by Vijit Jain from Citi. Manish, you can go 
ahead. 
 
Manish Adukia: Thanks, Anandita. Hi Vijay, Madhur, good to chat with you. First, a couple of follow-ups from 
the earlier discussion you were having to Sachin's questions. When you mentioned you want to go all in on 
market share, one, is that comment specific to consumer market share or is that broad based? 
 
Vijay Shekhar Sharma: Consumer market share and merchant market share both are there, Manish. The idea is 
that whenever we are talking market share and market share cap, we are talking about consumers. So 
whenever I'm quoting specifically, it is for consumer. ​In merchant, we are all in and it will be awkward for us to 
lose some share. 
 
Manish Adukia: And when you say you want to go all in on market share, what will drive that? 
 
Vijay Shekhar Sharma: We need to acquire customers in different ways and segments where there is some or 
other thing, whether it is marketing spends, whether it is collaborative partnerships, whether it is a product 
feature, whether there is something new in sight. So my thing is that I don't want to do it based on only 
marketing spends if you will, or cashback burn. I want to do it on product and features. I mean, we partnered 
with Perplexity at one point in time, if you remember. I was thinking that there will be large usage, but yeah, 
there is a lot on the table. We don't look at our consumer market share as people coming only for UPI 
payments.  
 
Manish Adukia: Very clear. My second question is before the MDR implementation was pushed from 15th 
October to post-Diwali, can you give us a peek into the kind of conversations you were having with your 
merchants? I'm just trying to understand the operational implementation of UPI MDR. Whenever it happens, 
let's say post-Diwali, when you go to, let's say, a merchant and the cap is at 40 basis points, by default, does 

everybody get switched on at 40 basis points? Or is there like, a bilateral negotiation you need to have with 
each merchant to say that, hey, you will pay 40, you will pay 30? Like, I'm just trying to think that from an 
operational implementation perspective, how heavy is it? Or can it happen at the flip of a switch on day one? 
 
Vijay Shekhar Sharma: Flip of a switch on day one. 
 
Manish Adukia: Okay, so you don't necessarily need to go and speak to your merchant and tell them that, hey, 
it's happening. You can just do it, and then negotiation can happen later. 
 
Vijay Shekhar Sharma: There's no negotiation. We work with small businesses. Big business owners have big 
tantrums; we don’t. Our business is very straightforward. Small merchant, small job, switch it on, done. And if 
you are like, let's say, a large merchant, you would like to negotiate that, oh my God, I would like to pay a lesser 
price. Then somebody else will enter with that price. I mean, even then, you will negotiate only when 
somebody else enters. So a small merchant is easier and a better, superior business always. And it is complex to 
do it. 
 
Manish Adukia: Right, so based on that statement, can I say that the majority of your GMV transactions, et 
cetera, should be closer to that 40 bps cap rather than a much lower number than that? 
 
Vijay Shekhar Sharma: Yes, but it will come only when you have transactions of more than 2000 rupees. 
 
Manish Adukia: Understand, got it. And last question on just the growth momentum in the business. This 
quarter, of course, you had very strong growth across businesses - financial services, marketing, payments - 
and your commentary suggests that financial services near term looks good. Marketing has recovered, 
payments, festivity, et cetera. So I'm just trying to think that across the various businesses that you have, are 
there any businesses where, in the near term, there's any growth headwind at all? And in the past, Madhur, 
and I know this is like, maybe more than a year back, you had guided for revenue growth in the 20s to sustain 
the medium term. Given what you've seen in the business in the last couple of quarters, and I'm talking ex of 
MDR, has that expectation of revenue growth momentum reset upwards? If you can, maybe talk about that. 
 
Madhur Deora: Yeah, so yes, we have now seen two consistent quarters of 28% growth. And while we stick by 
the reported numbers, if you exclude PIDF from the previous year's same quarters, this number is in the 30s. So 
we are seeing, thanks for pointing out, a strong tailwind. And we have said last quarter that across the board - 
consumer and merchant, payments and financial services, if you think about it that way. And we are seeing 
very healthy tailwinds in lending business. Personal loans, as we come out of the credit cycle, which was our 
expectation four or five quarters ago when we were in the middle of the credit cycle, like Vijay pointed out, it 
was a personal loan distribution business. The merchant loan business continues to do very well, including 
some TAM expansion opportunities that we have talked about, both on the slightly smaller ticket size, as well 
as the larger ticket size, around the whole business that we have been doing for the last seven years. 
 
And on payments, we see GMV growth, market share growth, as well as better pricing. And all of this excluding 
MDR, of course. So far, so far really well. I think a lot of sharper execution is also possible because of AI, 
because we do have a large cost structure on sales, on collection, on service, and so on. All of these things just 
become better RoI due to AI. And some of that shows up in better costs; some of those in faster revenue. So 
some of this does show up in faster revenue. So if we collect better, it shows up in higher revenue in our 
business model, as you understand it. And that's just to give an example. 
 
I think there are some very small, much smaller parts of the businesses where there are a few headwinds. So, 
for example, our equity trading business is doing quite well; equity broking, rather, is doing quite well on MTF. 

But overall market volumes haven't been that great. So that hasn't quite scaled up as much as we would like to. 
Travel has been a little bit sort of on and off. So there are headwinds in the travel industry as well. And there's 
been a little bit of headwind overall in wealth, including the gold business. So these are much, much smaller 
businesses of ours, but because you asked, and I just want to be complete. But in 85-90% of our revenue, we 
are seeing significant tailwinds rather than any meaningful headwinds. 
 
Manish Adukia: Thank you for answering my questions. All the best. 
 
Moderator: Thanks, Manish. We will take the next question from Vijit, followed by Pranav Kshatriya from 
Emkay. 
 
Vijit Jain: Yeah, hi, thanks. Hi, Vijay. Congratulations. Good set of numbers, I think. My first question, just a 
follow-up on the MDR thing to what Manish asked earlier. In general, do you think the industry readiness is 
there for MDR to be switched on immediately post-Diwali in terms of, I know there were discussions around 
some outstanding points of clarification that were needed from NPCI, and there are various players in the 
payment ecosystem who are all supposed to be ready to kind of do the MDR you guys collect, but it needs to 
flow through properly into the system. So, in terms of that operational readiness, are we there yet for it to get 
switched on post-Diwali, any specific date? That's part one of my question. And then I'll follow up with the rest.  
 
Vijay Shekhar Sharma: We're ready. The industry is ready.  
 
Vijit Jain: The industry as well? Sorry, Vijay, I know you guys are. 
 
Vijay Shekhar Sharma: Industry plays a bigger role. We are one of the participants. We are ready. We can do it. 
We do it. We already make MDR base revenue, credit card on UPI, UPI credit line, which is postpaid; issuing, 
acquiring - everything is working. It works.  
 
Vijit Jain: Okay, got it. Perfect. My second question is-  
 
Vijay Shekhar Sharma: By the way, for industry also, I'll say it works. It's just one of the payment instruments 
called a bank account. So I'm sure, Vijit, if you go deeper, MDR on UPI is a slang word for MDR for bank 
payments on QR, which other payment methods already have MDR, as you know, on credit cards or credit 
lines, and so on. So the system for everybody is working, actually. 
 
Vijit Jain: Got it. So it just needs a decision on the date in that sense then. 
 
Madhur Deora: That's right.  
 
Vijit Jain: Got it. Perfect. My second question is on the devices business. Good to see another good quarter: 
700,000-odd devices rolled out in the quarter. Now I'm just wondering, you know, now that MDR is there, in 
terms of where you roll out devices, what kind of merchants you target? Is there any kind of change in who 
you'd want to target? Would you look at merchants who do more than 2000 rupees plus transactions 
specifically? and B, I know that there is this provision for improving penetration of devices in smaller tier 
towns, right? That's carved out in the UPI program from NPCI. And I know you guys have that capability and 
infrastructure already set in place. So is that where you would focus more of your device rollout plans on? 
 
So I just wanted to get a broader flavour on how you're looking at that part. And a related question to it is your 
H1 capex on device rollout- is that what I should use as a, you know, kind of a benchmark on what capex would 
look like now? 

 
Madhur Deora: So, Vijit, as we have said, the MDR on UPI is an upside to our business model. It is not 
fundamental to our business model. So I just refer back to that and explain what I mean, which is in the small 
merchant space, the primary business model remains the same, which is we acquire through payments and we 
offer financial services. At our current penetration rates and so on, the financial services revenue is significantly 
larger than either the fund or the MDR opportunity, et cetera, right? 
 
So the short answer is fundamentally the whole business does not change. In the very small merchant 
business, we'll actively not get distracted by the fact that there is some, perhaps, additional MDR opportunity 
because the bigger monetization and the payback period comes from financial services. End of the day, the AI 
models that we use for what we call ARMS, Acquisition, Retention, Monetization and Service, they throw up 
the insights as to, hey, put some more sales effort in this pincode, put some more service effort in that pincode, 
and they will factor in the small merchant fund, the MDR opportunity, just like today they factored in the RuPay 
credit card on UPI opportunity. So they will do that as an input, but I don't think fundamentally the model will 
throw up surprising new facts.  
 
On capex, yes, we have said it was about 400 crores on a kind of inward devices count basis, and we expect 
that to be the same. That number is a little bit higher than before, but we are focusing a huge amount on 
engagement and retention of high-quality and high-potential merchants because the payback periods are 
working so well that we just want to make sure that we have enough funnel of high-quality, highly engaged 
merchants going into financial services. 
 
Vijit Jain: Perfect, thank you so much, Madhur. My last question, on the net payment margins, right? Now, this 
is a quarter where there is no UPI, so it's just business ex-UPI net payment margins, and it's nine basis points. 
Just general sense there, because top-down, if I look at the industry data, credit card spends have been kind of 
soft, right? Both QoQ, YoY, nothing particularly interesting has happened, at least in the industry. And I know 
you guys have other drivers, credit card on UPI, Paytm Postpaid, and device subscription fees as well. So in 
general, in the 8.5 to 9 bps move that happened in this quarter, what would you attribute that to? 
 
Madhur Deora: I think part of it is a little bit higher. We have a certain threshold, certain type of merchants; 
what type of pricing do we want to make? So I think there's just a little bit of additional discipline around that 
number, which we have imposed. So that's one. And the second is we have other factors as well, where we are 
gaining good share, and we have had momentum for a while, things like EMI, DCC, etcetera, and the enterprise 
side. So it's a combination of a few different things. 
 
Vijit Jain: Got it, perfect. Thank you so much. And best of luck for the next quarter. 
 
Madhur Deora: Thank you as well.
